title: Statics and Torque
learning_objectives: State the first condition for equilibrium and use it to solve for unknown forces.
State the second condition for equilibrium and compute a moment.
Explain the stability of a body from the position of its centre of gravity.

sections.title: Introduction to Statics and Torque
objectives: Describe what statics studies and why the turning effect of a force matters.

misconceptions.claim: Statics is the study of moving objects.
misconceptions.correction: It is the study of objects at rest, and of the forces and moments that keep them there.

summary: Statics is the study of equilibrium.
A moment is the turning effect of a force about a pivot.
Two conditions decide whether a body is in equilibrium.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: The First Condition for Equilibrium
objectives: Use the first condition for equilibrium, that the net force is zero.
Resolve forces into components and apply the first condition in two dimensions.

misconceptions.claim: A body at rest has no forces acting on it.
misconceptions.correction: It has forces acting on it that balance, so the net force is zero.

misconceptions.claim: The normal force on a body resting on a floor is half its weight.
misconceptions.correction: The floor pushes up with a force equal to the weight, so the normal force is the whole weight.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-1, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers half the weight as an option.

misconceptions.claim: The normal force on a body resting on a floor is a tenth of its weight.
misconceptions.correction: It is the whole weight. The floor pushes up with exactly the force the weight pushes down.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-5, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the value with the mass alone.

summary: The first condition is that the vector sum of the forces is zero.
Balanced forces need not be equal pairs, they must sum to zero in every direction.
The forces need not act at the same point for this condition.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

authored_exercises.stem: A 10 N weight hangs at rest from a single vertical rope. Find the tension in the rope.
solution: The weight is at rest, so the net force is zero.
The upward tension must balance the downward weight.
Tension = 10 N.

authored_exercises.stem: Forces of 6 N east and 6 N west act on the same body. Find the net force.
solution: Take east as positive: +6 N and -6 N.
Add the forces: 6 - 6 = 0 N.
The forces balance, so the net force is zero.

authored_exercises.stem: A 20 kg sign hangs at rest from two vertical ropes. Find the tension in each rope. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
solution: The weight is W = mg = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N.
The two ropes share the load equally: 2T = 196 N.
T = 98 N in each rope.

sections.title: The Second Condition for Equilibrium
objectives: Use the second condition for equilibrium, that the net moment is zero.
Calculate the moment of a force about a chosen pivot and apply the principle of moments.

misconceptions.claim: If the forces balance, the body is in equilibrium.
misconceptions.correction: Only if the forces balance and the turning effects balance as well. A couple is a pair of forces that turn a body without changing its motion.

misconceptions.claim: The angle between the force and the arm does not change the moment.
misconceptions.correction: Only the component of the force perpendicular to the arm turns the body, so the moment is F d sin(theta).
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-2, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the moment with the angle ignored.

misconceptions.claim: The moment of a force is the force divided by the distance from the pivot.
misconceptions.correction: The moment is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-6, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the force divided by the distance as an option.

summary: The second condition is that the net moment about any pivot is zero.
A moment is force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
A couple turns a body and gives it no net force.

sections.title: Stability
objectives: Explain stability from the position of the centre of gravity relative to the base of support.
Distinguish stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium.

misconceptions.claim: A body is stable when its centre of gravity is high.
misconceptions.correction: It is stable when the centre of gravity is low, or when it lies over the base of support, so a small tilt raises it.

misconceptions.claim: A narrow base makes a body stable.
misconceptions.correction: A narrow base makes a body unstable. A body is stable when a small tilt raises its centre of gravity.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-7, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the narrow base as the stable case.

summary: Stable, unstable and neutral depend on the centre of gravity and the base of support.
Tilting a stable body raises its centre of gravity, so it falls back.
A hanging object is stable because its centre of gravity is below the pivot.

authored_exercises.stem: A uniform 4.0-m ladder weighing 120 N leans against a smooth (frictionless) vertical wall, making a 60° angle with the ground. A 600-N painter stands on the ladder 2.0 m along its length, measured from the base. (a) Taking torques about the base of the ladder, find the normal force the wall exerts on the ladder. (b) Find the friction force that the ground must exert on the ladder's feet.
authored_exercises.answer: (a) 210 N (b) 210 N (the ground also pushes up with 720 N)
solution: Torques about the base: the wall force acts 4.0 sin 60° = 3.46 m above the base; the ladder's weight acts 2.0 cos 60° = 1.0 m along the ground; the painter acts 2.0 cos 60° = 1.0 m along the ground.
Horizontal equilibrium: the friction force at the ground equals the wall's push, so f = 208 ≈ 210 N.

sections.title: Applications of Statics, Including Problem-Solving Strategies
objectives: Set up a statics problem by drawing the free-body diagram before writing any equation.
Solve a beam or ladder problem by combining the force and moment equations.

misconceptions.claim: You can write the equilibrium equations straight away.
misconceptions.correction: You draw the free-body diagram first, choose a pivot, and only then write the equations.

summary: Always draw the free-body diagram first.
Choose a pivot that removes an unknown force where you can.
Solve the force equations and the moment equations together.

authored_exercises.stem: Why is it useful to choose the pivot at the point where an unknown force acts?
authored_exercises.answer: That force then has zero moment about the pivot, so it drops out of the moment equation.
solution: A moment is force times perpendicular distance from the pivot.
If the distance is zero, the moment is zero.
Choosing that point removes the unknown from the equation.

authored_exercises.stem: A 2 m beam is pivoted at one end. A 30 N force acts perpendicular to the beam at 1.5 m from the pivot. Find the moment of the force.
solution: The force is perpendicular to the beam, so the perpendicular distance is 1.5 m.
Moment = force × distance = 30 × 1.5.
The moment is 45 N m.

sections.title: Simple Machines
objectives: Explain the mechanical advantage of a simple machine and compute it from the forces.
Calculate the mechanical advantage and efficiency of a simple machine.

misconceptions.claim: A machine multiplies the force applied.
misconceptions.correction: It trades force for distance, so it multiplies the force only when it moves the load less far, and the mechanical advantage says by how much.

summary: The mechanical advantage is the load over the effort.
No machine is better than the effort: the work in equals the work out.
Machines save force or save distance, never both.

conditions.text: The vector sum of the forces on the body is zero.
With d the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force.
The net moment about the pivot is zero.
For an ideal machine, where the work in equals the work out.

definition.text: The state of a body at rest or in uniform motion, with the net force and the net moment both zero.
The turning effect of a force about a pivot, equal to the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
A pair of equal and opposite forces whose lines of action are apart, which turns a body without moving its centre.
The point at which the whole weight of a body can be treated as acting.
The factor by which a machine multiplies the effort, equal to the load over the effort.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: The output work of a machine is the input work divided by the efficiency.
exam_traps.correction: The output work is the input work multiplied by the efficiency, and the mechanical advantage is the load over the effort.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers the value from dividing, and the answer is the value from multiplying.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: The mechanical advantage of a machine includes its efficiency.
exam_traps.correction: The mechanical advantage is the load over the effort. The efficiency is a separate ratio, and multiplying the two is not the mechanical advantage.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers the efficiency times the mechanical advantage, and the answer is the mechanical advantage alone.

sec-5:exr-34.answer: *F* L = 7350 N and *F* R = 2450 N; as the car drives to the right, *F* L decreases and *F* R increases.

sec-6:exr-42.stem: What is the mechanical advantage of a nail puller where you exert a force 45 cm from the pivot and the nail is 1.8 cm on the other side? What minimum force must you exert to apply a force of 1250 N to the nail?
solution: The mechanical advantage is the ratio of the effort distance to the load distance: $MA=45\ \mathrm{cm}/1.8\ \mathrm{cm}=25$.
The required effort force is $F_{\mathrm{effort}}=F_{\mathrm{load}}/MA=1250\ \mathrm{N}/25=50\ \mathrm{N}$.

sec-4:exr-40.stem: A horse stands facing a wall, with its feet 0.35 m horizontally from the wall. The wall pushes horizontally on the horse at a height of 1.20 m above the ground. The horse's center of mass is 1.40 m above the ground and midway between its feet. The total mass of the horse and rider is 500 kg. (a) Calculate the magnitude and direction of the force on each foot (two are on the ground). (b) What is the minimum coefficient of friction between the hooves and the ground?
solution: The weight is $W=mg=(500\ \mathrm{kg})(9.80\ \mathrm{m/s^{2}})=4.90\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N}$.

Take torques about the feet. The wall force acts at 1.20 m and the weight at 0.35 m horizontally, so $F_{\mathrm{wall}}(1.20)=(4.90\times10^{3})(0.35)$ and $F_{\mathrm{wall}}=1.43\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Each foot carries half the weight, $N=2.45\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N}$, and half the horizontal force, $f=7.15\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{N}$.
The resultant on each foot is $\sqrt{(2.45\times10^{3})^{2}+(7.15\times10^{2})^{2}}=2.55\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N}$, directed $\tan^{-1}(715/2450)=16.3^{\circ}$ from the vertical toward the wall.
(b) The minimum coefficient of friction is $\mu_{\min}=f/N=715/2450=0.292$.
